ratios.title: Single adults leaving shelter for a home, per 100 arriving
ratios.question: The report counts how many single adults enter the shelter system and, separately, how many leave it for permanent housing. It never puts the two side by side.
ratios.caveat: The people leaving in a year are not the people who arrived in it, so this is a comparison of two flows over the same fiscal year, not the share of any group that got housed. The entry count also excludes Safe Havens, veterans' short-term housing, and anyone returning within a year of a previous stay.
ratios.numLabel: Single adults exiting to permanent housing
ratios.denLabel: Single adults entering the DHS shelter services system

ratios.title: Families with children leaving shelter for a home, per 100 arriving
ratios.question: The same comparison for families with children, the population the shelter system grew fastest in.
ratios.caveat: Two flows over the same fiscal year, not a cohort. The entry figure counts families found eligible for shelter, which is not the same as families who applied.
ratios.numLabel: Families with children exiting to permanent housing
ratios.denLabel: Families with children entering the DHS shelter services system

ratios.title: Adult families leaving shelter for a home, per 100 arriving
ratios.question: The smallest of the three shelter populations, and the one least written about.
ratios.caveat: Two flows over the same fiscal year, not a cohort. Small counts, so single-year moves are noisy.
ratios.numLabel: Adult families exiting to permanent housing
ratios.denLabel: Adult families entering the DHS shelter services system

ratios.title: Single-adult exits that needed a housing subsidy, per 100 exits
ratios.question: Every exit from shelter to permanent housing is filed as either subsidised or unsubsidised. The split is printed; the share is not. It says how much of the city's rehousing now depends on a voucher.
ratios.caveat: A subsidised exit is not a worse outcome than an unsubsidised one. This measures what the exits rest on, not how good they are. Numerator and denominator are the same flow over the same fiscal year, so the share is exact.
ratios.numLabel: Single adults exiting to permanent housing — Subsidized
ratios.denLabel: Single adults exiting to permanent housing

ratios.title: Family exits that needed a housing subsidy, per 100 exits
ratios.question: The same split for families with children.
ratios.caveat: A subsidised exit is not a worse outcome than an unsubsidised one. Same flow, same fiscal year, so the share is exact.
ratios.numLabel: Families with children exiting to permanent housing — Subsidized
ratios.denLabel: Families with children exiting to permanent housing

ratios.title: Correction Department spending per person in custody
ratios.question: The report prints what the Department of Correction spends and, in another table, the average number of people it holds. The cost of a jail bed is the single most quoted number about Rikers and the report never states it.
ratios.caveat: A year of spending divided by the average number held on a day in that year. It is the Correction Department's own operating expenditure only: it leaves out fringe benefits, debt service, the health care Health + Hospitals delivers in the jails, and legal settlements, all of which sit in other agencies' budgets. Fully loaded estimates published by the Comptroller are far higher. Dollars are as published and not adjusted for inflation.
ratios.numLabel: Agency expenditures, as reported in the report's own resources table

ratios.title: Sanitation Department spending per ton of waste handled
ratios.question: The city published a refuse collection cost per ton until fiscal 2020 and then stopped. This is the nearest thing the current report still lets you build.
ratios.caveat: Not the cost of collecting a ton. The Sanitation Department's budget also covers street cleaning, snow, lot cleaning and enforcement, so this is total agency spending for a fiscal year divided by everything it disposed of or recycled in that same year. It is a different, larger number than the collection cost the city used to print, and the two should not be compared. Dollars are as published.
ratios.numLabel: Agency expenditures, as reported in the report's own resources table
ratios.denLabel: Tons of refuse disposed (000) plus Overall tons recycled (000)

ratios.title: Tons of waste handled per Sanitation Department employee
ratios.question: Tonnage and headcount are both printed, in different tables, and never divided.
ratios.caveat: A crude measure. Most Sanitation employees are not on a collection truck, and tonnage moves with what the city throws away rather than with how hard anyone works. Headcount is the fiscal year's reported personnel, uniformed and civilian together, against the same year's tonnage.
ratios.numLabel: Tons of refuse disposed (000) plus Overall tons recycled (000)
ratios.denLabel: Agency expenditures, as reported in the report's own resources table

ratios.title: Overtime as a share of Correction Department spending
ratios.question: Both figures sit in the agency resources table, one row apart. The share is the number that says how much of a jail system runs on overtime.
ratios.caveat: Overtime paid and total expenditures, both for the same fiscal year, both as published in the report's own resources table. It is a share of all agency spending, not of the payroll, so the payroll share is higher still.
ratios.numLabel: Agency expenditures, as reported in the report's own resources table
ratios.denLabel: Agency expenditures, as reported in the report's own resources table

ratios.title: Overtime as a share of Police Department spending
ratios.question: The same question for the city's largest uniformed agency.
ratios.caveat: Overtime paid and total expenditures for the same fiscal year, as published. A share of all agency spending, not of the payroll.
ratios.numLabel: Agency expenditures, as reported in the report's own resources table
ratios.denLabel: Agency expenditures, as reported in the report's own resources table

ratios.title: Overtime as a share of Fire Department spending
ratios.question: And for the Fire Department, which runs the ambulances too.
ratios.caveat: Overtime paid and total expenditures for the same fiscal year, as published. A share of all agency spending, not of the payroll.
ratios.numLabel: Agency expenditures, as reported in the report's own resources table
ratios.denLabel: Agency expenditures, as reported in the report's own resources table

ratios.title: Nonemergency building complaints responded to, per 100 received
ratios.question: The Buildings Department prints how many nonemergency complaints it takes in and how many it goes out to, on the same page, without the share.
ratios.caveat: Responding means an inspector made an initial field visit, not that anyone got inside or that anything was resolved. Both counts cover the same fiscal year but do not follow the same complaints, so a backlog worked off later lands in a later year's numerator.
ratios.numLabel: Priority B (nonemergency) complaints responded to

ratios.title: Emergency building complaints responded to, per 100 received
ratios.question: The same sum for the complaints the department treats as emergencies, which is the comparison that makes the nonemergency figure mean something.
ratios.caveat: Same fiscal year on both sides, and the same caution: responding means a field visit was made, not that the hazard was fixed.
ratios.numLabel: Priority A (emergency) complaints responded to

ratios.title: Graffiti requests closed, per 100 received
ratios.question: Received and closed are both printed. The share is not.
ratios.caveat: Both counts are for the same fiscal year but not the same requests, so a figure near or above 100 means the agency cleared roughly as many as came in, not that every request was handled.
ratios.numLabel: Graffiti service requests closed

ratios.title: Housing violations closed, per 100 issued
ratios.question: Housing Preservation and Development issues hundreds of thousands of violations a year and closes a comparable number. Whether it is keeping up is not printed.
ratios.caveat: Closures in a fiscal year against violations issued in that same year, and they are not the same violations. Above 100 means the agency closed more than it issued that year, which means it worked into a backlog; below 100 means the backlog grew. It does not mean any particular violation was fixed.
ratios.numLabel: Violations closed

ratios.title: Complaints against officers substantiated, per 100 cases closed
ratios.question: The Civilian Complaint Review Board publishes how many cases it closes and, separately, how many it closes as substantiated. The substantiation rate that follows is the number everyone argues about, and it is not printed.
ratios.caveat: Both are closures in the same fiscal year, but the board counts complaints and cases in slightly different units: the nine published closure categories sum to within about one and a half per cent of the total cases closed, not exactly to it. Read this as close to the substantiation rate rather than as it.
ratios.numLabel: Substantiated complaints closed

ratios.title: Major felony arrests per 100 major felonies reported
ratios.question: Both figures are printed in the police chapter, a few rows apart, and never divided.
ratios.caveat: Not a clearance rate and not a solve rate. Both counts cover the same fiscal year but not the same crimes: an arrest made this year may be for a crime reported in an earlier one, a single crime can produce several arrests or none, and an arrest is not a conviction. One further wrinkle: the printed report restated the major felony count for fiscal 2022 to 2025 by about a fifth of a per cent, so the years to 2025 use the open data figures and fiscal 2026 uses the report's.
ratios.numLabel: Major felony crime arrests

ratios.title: Public housing placements that went to homeless applicants, per 100
ratios.question: The Housing Authority prints how many applicants it places and, separately, how many of those came from the shelter system. The share is the rationing decision.
ratios.caveat: Same flow, same fiscal year, so the share is exact. It says how placements were allocated, not whether there were enough of them.
ratios.numLabel: Homeless applicants placed in public housing — NYCHA housing

ratios.title: Medallion taxi inspections passed, per 100 conducted
ratios.question: Taxi and Limousine prints inspections conducted and inspections passed. The pass rate is the number that says what condition the fleet is in.
ratios.caveat: Same inspections, same fiscal year, so the rate is exact. A failed inspection is usually re-presented after repair, so this is a first-pass rate rather than the share of cabs that end up roadworthy.
ratios.numLabel: Medallion taxi safety and emissions inspections conducted – Passed
ratios.denLabel: Medallion taxi safety and emissions inspections conducted – Total

ratios.title: Items borrowed per active Brooklyn library card
ratios.question: Circulation and active cards are both printed, both in thousands. How much the average active borrower actually borrows is not.
ratios.caveat: Read the level, not the trend. Both figures cover the same fiscal year, but the active-card count moves in a way no borrowing pattern explains -- Brooklyn reports 846,000 active cards in fiscal 2021 and 494,000 in fiscal 2022 -- which means the definition has been changed more than once. Comparing the three library systems against each other in the same year is sound; reading the line as a change in how much people borrow is not. An active card is also a card, not a person, and circulation includes renewals and e-book loans.
ratios.numLabel: Circulation (000)

ratios.title: Items borrowed per active New York Public Library card
ratios.question: The same sum for the system covering Manhattan, the Bronx and Staten Island.
ratios.caveat: Read the level, not the trend: the active-card count is redefined more than once across this run, which is why the line moves more than borrowing does. The New York Public Library reports 522,000 active cards in fiscal 2021 and 1,327,000 in fiscal 2024. Comparing the three systems in the same year is sound.
ratios.numLabel: Circulation (000)

ratios.title: Items borrowed per active Queens library card
ratios.question: And for Queens, which lets the three systems be read against one another.
ratios.caveat: Read the level, not the trend, for the same reason as the other two systems: the active-card count is redefined more than once across this run. Comparing Queens, Brooklyn and the New York Public Library in the same year is the sound use of it.
ratios.numLabel: Circulation (000)

ratios.title: Potholes repaired per pothole work order
ratios.question: Transportation prints how many pothole work orders it opens and, separately, how many potholes it fills on local streets and on the arterial system. One order clearly covers more than one hole, and the report never says how many.
ratios.caveat: Repairs and orders are both counted over the same fiscal year but are not tied to one another in the data: a crew sent to one order may fill holes nobody reported. Read it as filling intensity, not as a productivity rate.
ratios.numLabel: Potholes repaired on local streets only plus Potholes repaired on arterial highway system
